notes: The problem is not a universally small budget: some failing runs allow 64,000–128,000 output tokens. Certain reasoning settings consume that allowance before the final answer. Across 19,500 attempts, 925 hit an output limit; 851 of those have empty final answers. Limits therefore bind very differently across models and settings, and these runs do not reliably measure performance near each model’s ceiling.

The common setup supplies one text-encoded board position, asks for one move, and provides no tools or feedback. Model-specific provider options control reasoning effort and output length. The chess engine used for reference checks is not available to evaluated models. This is a test of unaided text-based move selection, not chess-engine use.

notes: All 100 positions and solutions are publicly available by the review date. They were generated with randomized openings, which plausibly reduced overlap with existing chess puzzles at creation. Public release now permits memorization by later models; training-data contamination was not established.

Epoch reports that five chess players rated approximately 1700–2400 attempted a randomly chosen 20-puzzle set without engines. Scores ranged from 40% to 75%, with one accidentally exposed answer excluded. This supports human feasibility on a subset, not all 100 puzzles or an average-person baseline. Ratings mix online and over-the-board scales; one player omitted timing.

notes: Of 193 log files, 191 contain one attempt per puzzle and two contain two. Different reasoning settings are not independent repeats of the same configuration. With only 100 puzzles, small score differences are uncertain; the supplied runs do not provide five-repeat estimates of run-to-run variability.

Scores directly measure selection of an engine-preferred move from a text-encoded chess position. This plausibly involves planning and board-state reasoning, but also depends on chess knowledge and reading the encoding. A single move does not establish full-game playing strength or general spatial reasoning. Only the final move is scored, not the correctness of the explanation.
